title: Micropost-integrated acoustofluidic device for enhanced microparticle trapping and release
content: Acoustofluidics is a powerful tool in the development of devices to focus, trap, or otherwise manipulate microparticles for many uses in materials processing, biomedical analysis, and sample preparation. Most approaches have used the primary acoustic force for positioning and trapping, but this force is dramatically weaker as particles move into the nanoscale. This has driven interest in trapping of particles to surfaces using the acoustic secondary force, which has enabled creation of both acoustically enhanced filters and acoustic trapping via seed particles, effectively trapping particles at the nanoscale. These approaches remain constrained by fluidic drag and limited residence-time control within acoustic fields. To obviate these concerns, we recently demonstrated that positioning a wire at the acoustic pressure node of a cylindrical microcapillary enables efficient particle capture. While promising, this approach limits the types of device geometry that can be considered. Therefore, here we expanded upon this concept and demonstrated microfabricated posts positioned at the pressure node can enhance particle capture via primary and secondary acoustic forces. Primary acoustic forces drive microparticles toward the posts, where secondary acoustic interactions and reduced near-wall flow velocities facilitate stable capture. In addition, particle–particle interactions involving acoustically trapped particles, as well as particle–surface interactions, may also play a role in enhancing the capture efficiency. This work demonstrates that the concept of placing microstructures in predicted nodes will be an effective method for developing acoustic trapping devices of microparticles. The acoustofluidic device with microposts discussed herein is capable of capturing 11.1 µm particles with a 93% capture rate, and 35–55 fold particle enrichment, and may provide a basis for future development toward submicron and nanoscale particle trapping. Furthermore, the flexibility of microfabrication geometries offers the possibility of using this approach for more complex trapping assembly that may be of value in numerous micromaterials fabrication applications.
